We detected 2 potential power analyses.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as ‘post-hoc’. Calculating observed power is almost never useful. If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

power_id text
1 To test whether the non-significant simple effects indicate the absence of a difference, we conducted TOST equivalence tests (not preregistered). For each effect, the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) was set to the bound at which the TOST procedure has 80% power at α = .05 when the true effect is zero, given that effect’s empirical SE. In the actual advice condition, the influence of AI and human advice was statistically equivalent: we can reject source differences larger than 0.048 WOA units, t(1881) = -1.82, p = .034. For AI advice, the influence expected in the hypothetical condition was equivalent to the influence observed in the actual condition at the group level: we can reject mode differences larger than 0.066, t(625) = -1.84, p = .033. For human advice, the test was inconclusive (SESOI = 0.066, t(636) = 1.42, p = .077): expected influence was somewhat higher than actual influence, but this difference was neither significant nor demonstrably absent. Taken together, participants expected less influence from AI than from human advice, whereas both sources were equally influential when advice was actually received.
2 401 participants completed the survey on prolific.com. Inclusion criteria were being a native English speaker, having an approval rate of at least 95% of previous surveys on the platform, and not having participated in previous studies using similar material. Target sample size (N = 400) was determined by a power simulation based on pilot data (see OSF repository for code). In a linear model predicting weight of advice from advice mode, advice source, and their interaction, this sample size should yield over 80% power to detect a positive interaction coefficient of 𝛽 = 0.07 (as underestimating weight of advice more for AI than for humans would be indicated by a significant interaction effect in this design). Participants were paid ￡1.20 for an estimated 8 minutes of their time (￡9/hour). 11 Participants were excluded for failing the Müller-Lyer illusion, leaving a final sample size of 390 valid responses (mean age = 42.52 years, SD = 12.97 years, 192 female, 192 male, 1 non-binary, 1 another gender, 2 prefer not to say, 2 missing). Of the 384 participants with available ethnicity data, the majority identified as White (273), followed by Black (69), Asian (25), Mixed (12), and Other (5). Of the 388 participants with available residence data, most resided in the United Kingdom (232) or the United States (82), followed by Canada (24), South Africa (22), Australia (13), and Ireland (8); 7 resided in other countries.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 60 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
ps >= .07 Two features significantly predicted WOA: Flesch-Kincaid grade level, and average sentence length; none of the remaining eight reached significance (all other ps >= .07).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 73 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 0 of 66 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 66 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (73 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents id, scenario_num, scenario_title while the data has id, scenario_num, scenario_title. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 30 codebook/README/label sources and 66 data columns across 3 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (73 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents id, scenario_num, scenario_title while the data has id, scenario_num, scenario_title. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 30 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (12), Jupyter checkpoints (12), operating system (4), R history (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 34 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .727 Pairwise contrasts confirmed that Care and Fairness did not differ from each other (p = .727), nor did Authority and Sanctity (p = .897), but all other foundation pairs differed significantly (all ps < .001, Holm-corrected).

p = .270 Decomposing the interaction the other way (not preregistered) showed that the source difference was located in expectations: participants in the hypothetical condition rated AI advice as less influential than human advice (b = -0.040, SE = 0.016, t(1835) = -2.57, p = .010), whereas in the actual condition, AI and human advice did not differ in influence (b = 0.018, SE = 0.016, t(1884) = 1.10, p = .270).
p = .077 For human advice, the test was inconclusive (SESOI = 0.066, t(636) = 1.42, p = .077): expected influence was somewhat higher than actual influence, but this difference was neither significant nor demonstrably absent.
p = .195 First, when retaining the full range of defined WOA values rather than restricting to [0, 1] (M human = 0.30, SD = 0.94; M AI = 0.35, SD = 1.49 in the actual condition), adding the source × mode interaction no longer improved model fit (χ²(1) = 1.68, p = .195; b = 0.10, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.052, 0.255]).
p = .428 Because the unbounded actual WOA values greatly inflate residual variance, the source difference in the hypothetical condition, whose data are unchanged by this treatment, was also no longer significant in this model (b AI = -0.05, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.157, 0.066], p = .428).
p = .911 Among the few who did revise, movements split roughly evenly upward vs. downward for both sources (human: 3 up, 4 down; AI: 2 up, 2 down), with no difference between human and AI advice, χ²(2) = 0.19, p = .911.
p = .436 Under the WOA = 1 coding, it did not (χ²(1) = 0.61, p = .436; b = 0.02, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.031, 0.071]).

p = .501 First, in a mixed-effects model predicting WOA from centroid distance (how far an individual text’s embedding sits from the average embedding for that scenario, random intercepts for participant and scenario), the effect was non-significant (b centroid distance = -0.106, SE = 0.108, 95% CI [-0.318, 0.106], p = .329), and adding an interaction with advice source did not improve model fit over the additive model (χ²(1) = 0.45, p = .501).
p = .264 Second, we tested mean pairwise distance (how semantically spread out advice texts are within a given scenario and source, a coarser, group-level rather than per-text measure), which also did not predict WOA (b pairwise distance = -0.079, SE = 0.071, 95% CI [-0.217, 0.059], p = .264) and did not interact with source (χ²(1) = 1.99, p = .159).

p = .527 Adding source as a main effect to this model did not improve fit (χ²(1) = 0.40, p = .527), and letting each foundation’s effect vary by source did not improve fit further either (χ²(5) = 5.86, p = .320).
p = .320 Adding source as a main effect to this model did not improve fit (χ²(1) = 0.40, p = .527), and letting each foundation’s effect vary by source did not improve fit further either (χ²(5) = 5.86, p = .320).
p = .253 Adding source as a main effect did not improve fit over the virtue/vice-only model (χ²(1) = 1.31, p = .253), but adding the source interaction did (χ²(2) = 7.54, p = .023), driven specifically by the source × vice term (see Table 7).

For AI advice, the influence expected in the hypothetical condition was equivalent to the influence observed in the actual condition at the group level: we can reject mode differences larger than 0.066, t(625) = -1.84, p = .033.
For human advice, the test was inconclusive (SESOI = 0.066, t(636) = 1.42, p = .077): expected influence was somewhat higher than actual influence, but this difference was neither significant nor demonstrably absent.
Extremity significantly improved fit over source alone (χ²(1) = 5.32, p = .021) and independently predicted somewhat greater uptake (b extremity = 0.0018, SE = 0.0008, 95% CI [0.0003, 0.0034], t(911) = 2.31, p = .021).

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 1 code file.

File name setwd() calls found

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 66 columns across 3 data files.

Issues Identified

3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script uses a location that exists only on your computer.

  • _inline_csv.py reads h://Meine Ablage//moral advisors//OSF repo//exp 2 - advice taking study//materials//local demo//human_and_GPT_advice.csv.
  • generate_scenario_overview.py reads h://Meine Ablage//moral advisors//OSF repo//exp 2 - advice taking study//materials//local demo//human_and_GPT_advice.csv.

No other computer has that folder, and the file is also not in the deposit.

  1. Add the file to the deposit.
  2. In the script, write the location from the top folder of your project, such as data/survey.csv. In R, here::here(“data”, “survey.csv”) does this for you.
  3. Remove any setwd() lines.

Your code was written for older versions of its packages.

  • llm advice elicitation.ipynb: “AttributeError: module ‘openai’ has no attribute ‘langfuse_auth_check’”

A function or option has changed since you wrote the code, so it stops with today’s version of the package.

  1. In R, run renv::init() in your project and add the renv.lock file this creates to the deposit; in Python, run pip freeze > requirements.txt and add that file.
  2. State your version of R or Python in the README.
  3. Better still, update the code so it also works with current versions.

A script uses an online service that needs a personal key.

  • robustness_scoring.py

Say in the README which service it is and how to get a key. Services change or close (Dark Sky has closed), so also save the data the script downloads, add it to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copy.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • exp 1 - advice elicitation/humans/data/main/00_data-wrangling.Rmd: Status
  • 01_sample-demographics.R: mutate
  • 02_text_analyses.R: corpus

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • 02_power-sim.qmd
  • 02_power-sim.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

  • 03_getting_embeddings.py
  • exp 2 - advice taking study/data/main/00_data-wrangling.Rmd

The error message of each script is in the table above.

Other problems in the files

  • 05_run_emfd.py calls os.chdir(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.
  • 06_text_analyses_mfd.Rmd calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.
  • eMFDscore_Tutorial.ipynb holds notebook commands that are not Python (%%bash; %%bash; %%bash; %%bash; %%bash; %%bash). We left them out so the code could run; what they install or prepare was not done.
  • llm advice elicitation.ipynb holds notebook commands that are not Python (!pip install -q langfuse pandas). We left them out so the code could run; what they install or prepare was not done.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 23 scripts: 7 ran without error, 4 errored, 2 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 3 scripts could not be tried, because a file they need was not downloaded: 00_data-wrangling.R, 03_merge-human-GPT.qmd, 07_demographics.Rmd. They are not counted as scripts that did not reproduce. Undefined-variable errors

3 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

File Missing variable Defined in
exp 1 - advice elicitation/humans/data/main/00_data-wrangling.Rmd Status (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)
01_sample-demographics.R mutate (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)
02_text_analyses.R corpus (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)

setwd() in the code

1 script calls setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reproducible after removing setwd(): 06_text_analyses_mfd.Rmd.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set
06_text_analyses_mfd.Rmd 1 (non-literal)

library() calls added

1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself. The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run it we added the library() calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after adding library() calls it should make itself.

> set.seed(1)
> cond <- c("hypothetical","actual")
> src  <- c("human","ai")
> mu   <- matrix(
>   c(0.30, 0.20,   # hypothetical: human, ai
>     0.25, 0.40),  # actual:       human, ai
>   nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
>   dimnames = list(cond, src)
> )
> n_per_cell <- 100
> sd <- 0.10
> dat <- expand.grid(condition = cond, source = src, i = seq_len(n_per_cell))
> dat$WOA <- rnorm(nrow(dat), mean = mapply(function(c,s) mu[c,s], dat$condition, dat$source), sd = sd)
> dat$i <- NULL
> dat$condition <- factor(dat$condition, levels = c("hypothetical","actual"))
> dat$source    <- factor(dat$source,    levels = c("human","ai"))
> raw <- with(dat, tapply(WOA, list(condition, source), mean))
> HH <- raw["hypothetical","human"]
> HA <- raw["hypothetical","ai"]
> AH <- raw["actual","human"]
> AA <- raw["actual","ai"]
> beta_raw <- c(
>   "(Intercept)"              = HH,                     # baseline cell
>   "conditionactual"          = AH - HH,                # (actual - hypothetical) @ human
>   "sourceai"                 = HA - HH,                # (ai - human) @ hypothetical
>   "conditionactual:sourceai" = (AA - HA) - (AH - HH)   # difference-in-differences
> )
> m <- lm(WOA ~ condition * source, data = dat)
> beta_mod <- coef(m)[names(beta_raw)]
> print(round(rbind(raw_contrasts = beta_raw, model_coefs = beta_mod), 6))

Degrees-of-freedom method: kenward-roger 
> set.seed(1)
> cond <- c("hypothetical","actual")
> src  <- c("human","ai")
> mu   <- matrix(
>   c(0.30, 0.20,   # hypothetical: human, ai
>     0.25, 0.40),  # actual:       human, ai
>   nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
>   dimnames = list(cond, src)
> )
> n_per_cell <- 100
> sd <- 0.10
> dat <- expand.grid(condition = cond, source = src, i = seq_len(n_per_cell))
> dat$WOA <- rnorm(nrow(dat), mean = mapply(function(c,s) mu[c,s], dat$condition, dat$source), sd = sd)
> dat$i <- NULL
> dat$condition <- factor(dat$condition, levels = c("hypothetical","actual"))
> dat$source    <- factor(dat$source,    levels = c("human","ai"))
> raw <- with(dat, tapply(WOA, list(condition, source), mean))
> HH <- raw["hypothetical","human"]
> HA <- raw["hypothetical","ai"]
> AH <- raw["actual","human"]
> AA <- raw["actual","ai"]
> beta_raw <- c(
>   "(Intercept)"              = HH,                     # baseline cell
>   "conditionactual"          = AH - HH,                # (actual - hypothetical) @ human
>   "sourceai"                 = HA - HH,                # (ai - human) @ hypothetical
>   "conditionactual:sourceai" = (AA - HA) - (AH - HH)   # difference-in-differences
> )
> m <- lm(WOA ~ condition * source, data = dat)
> beta_mod <- coef(m)[names(beta_raw)]
> print(round(rbind(raw_contrasts = beta_raw, model_coefs = beta_mod), 6))
              (Intercept) conditionactual  sourceai conditionactual:sourceai
raw_contrasts     0.29153       -0.030233 -0.079474                 0.218528
model_coefs       0.29153       -0.030233 -0.079474                 0.218528

</table>> run_lrt <- function(score_col, label) {
> 
>   d <- merged |>
>     mutate(score = if_else(advice_source == "human",
>                            score_original,
>                            .data[[score_col]])) |>
>     filter(!is.na(score), !is.na(scenario_num)) |>
>     mutate(
>       advice_source = factor(advice_source, levels = c("human", "ai")),
>       pro_contra    = factor(pro_contra,    levels = c("pro", "contra"))
>     )
> 
>   m_null <- lmer(score ~ 1                          + (1 | scenario_num), d, REML = FALSE)
>   m_dir  <- lmer(score ~ pro_contra                 + (1 | scenario_num), d, REML = FALSE)
>   m_add  <- lmer(score ~ advice_source + pro_contra + (1 | scenario_num), d, REML = FALSE)
>   m_int  <- lmer(score ~ advice_source * pro_contra + (1 | scenario_num), d, REML = FALSE)
> 
>   # Sequential LRT table (drop the baseline null row which has no chi-sq)
>   lrt_tbl <- anova(m_null, m_dir, m_add, m_int) |>
>     as_tibble(rownames = "model") |>
>     filter(!is.na(Chisq)) |>
>     transmute(
>       Comparison = c("+ direction (pro/contra)",
>                      "+ source (human/AI)",
>                      "+ direction × source"),
>       `χ²(1)`    = round(Chisq, 2),
>       p          = fmt_p(`Pr(>Chisq)`)
>     )
> 
>   # Fixed-effect coefficients from the interaction model
>   coef_tbl <- summary(m_int)$coefficients |>
>     as_tibble(rownames = "Term") |>
>     rename(B = Estimate, SE = `Std. Error`, t = `t value`) |>
>     mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 2)))
> 
>   list(label = label, n = nrow(d), lrt = lrt_tbl, coefs = coef_tbl)
> }
> lrt_results <- map2(score_vars, score_labels, run_lrt)
> for (i in seq_along(lrt_results)) {
>   res <- lrt_results[[i]]
> 
>   cat(sprintf("\n### %s  (n = %d)\n\n", res$label, res$n))
> 
>   cat(kbl(res$lrt, format = "html",
>           caption = sprintf("Sequential LRTs — %s scoring", res$label)) |>
>         style_tbl() |>
>         as.character())
> 
>   cat("\n\n**Interaction model fixed effects (m_int):**\n\n")
> 
>   cat(kbl(res$coefs, format = "html") |>
>         style_tbl() |>
>         as.character())
> 
>   cat("\n\n---\n\n")
> }

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> + source (human/AI) </td>

os.chdir() in the code

1 script calls os.chdir(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with pass. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring an os.chdir() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Dependencies were installed into a throwaway library before running (pip install): 9 succeeded, 0 failed. langfuse, nltk, openai, pandas, progressbar, python-dotenv, scikit-learn, spacy, tqdm were installed.

Duplicate files across repo mirrors

16 files are byte-identical to another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component that mirrors the same materials). Reported vs. reproduced

106 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 6 matched (5 fully, 1 partially) — 5.7% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

1 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook file bundles the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the file itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 24 result tables (405 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Participants were equally influenced by human and AI moral advice, revising their judgments by a little under a third of the distance to the advice.

In a foundational series of (pre-GPT) studies, Bigman and Gray (2018) found that participants were reluctant to let machines make morally consequential decisions in areas such as medicine, law, warfare, and autonomous driving, a pattern they linked in part to the perception that machines lack the kind of “mind” needed for legitimate moral judgment.

Although participants were often indifferent or somewhat averse to algorithmic advice in hypothetical reports, they relied on it as much as or more than human advice in actual judgment tasks.

In a second study, a new sample of participants completed a Judge-Advisor System task using a subset of these scenarios.

All participants provided informed consent before participation.

For each scenario, participants were randomly assigned to write advice either pro or contra an action that the agent in the scenario was considering (“Write persuasive advice explaining why it is [not] acceptable for Maya to say no to lending Rachel the money”).

This task was incentivized: Participants were informed that their writing would be used in a future advice-taking study, and that they could earn a bonus of 3 if one of their pieces of advice would be among the top 10 percent of the most convincing pieces of advice.

Participants had to correctly answer an instruction check within two attempts before starting the main task (“Which of the following is TRUE about this study?”

After completing the survey, we asked again whether they had used any AI tools (and if so, for what), emphasizing that this would not affect the approval of their submission on prolific.com, but merely inform our interpretation of the data.

101 participants completed the survey on prolific.com.

Participants had to be native English speakers, have an approval rate of previous studies on the platform of at least 95%, and not have participated in previous studies using the same materials.

Participants were paid ￡3 for an estimated 15 minutes of their time (￡12/hour).

Seven participants were excluded for failing the first attention check, one for failing the Müller-Lyer bot check, and one because their text was flagged as AI-generated by gptzero.me.

Participants were randomly assigned to either the actual or the hypothetical advice condition.

The six scenarios shown to one participant were randomly drawn from the full set of 24 scenarios, without replacement.

“Advice from AI (GPT-4)”), and the numerical acceptability score was presented below the advice, visualized as a selected value on a sliding scale like the one participants had used on the previous page.

After reading the advice and continuing to the next page, participants were asked for a second moral judgment of the case (“Please evaluate the scenario once more”).

Instead, participants were simply asked: “To what extent could advice from previous study participants [a Large Language Model (e.g., ChatGPT)] change your opinion about this situation?”, rated on a numbered sliding scale ranging from 0 (“not at all”) to 100 (“fully”).

After completing all six scenarios, participants completed a 12-item “Attitudes towards AI” survey (Stein et al., 2024) before the experiment ended with a debriefing and the assessment of demographic variables.

401 participants completed the survey on prolific.com.

Participants were paid ￡1.20 for an estimated 8 minutes of their time (￡9/hour).

11 Participants were excluded for failing the Müller-Lyer illusion, leaving a final sample size of 390 valid responses (mean age = 42.52 years, SD = 12.97 years, 192 female, 192 male, 1 non-binary, 1 another gender, 2 prefer not to say, 2 missing).

Thus, across advisor types, participants were somewhat more persuaded by linguistically more complex advice.

How semantically typical or unusual an advice text is, whether at the level of the individual text or the advisor group, appears to be orthogonal to how much participants are persuaded by it.

In the actual advice condition of our study, participants were equally influenced by human and AI advice, revising their moral judgments by just under 30% of the distance between their initial position and the advice score, regardless of source (27% for humans, 28% for AI).

In addition, since each piece of advice consisted of a written paragraph together with a numerical acceptability score, we cannot say which component did the work, i.e., whether participants were persuaded by the text or were simply anchoring on the number.

Second, our participants did not choose to receive moral advice: they were simply presented with it.

Ethics approval statement:

This set of two studies received ethical approval from the Institutional Review Board of [blinded for peer review], approval number LIP-2024-08, prior to data collection.

research_questions Participants read a set of realistic moral scenarios and are asked to write persuasive advice either in favor of or against the acceptability of the focal action (e.g., staying silent when witnessing inappropriate behavior). They are instructed to produce high-quality, convincing advice directed at future participants (financially incentivized for persuasiveness). After writing each advice paragraph, participants rate (a) the degree to which their advice conveys that the action is morally acceptable, and (b) how morally acceptable they personally find the action, both on 0–100 scales (0 = not acceptable at all, 100 = fully acceptable). Each participant completes multiple randomly selected scenarios from a larger pool. The goal is to collect human-generated advice texts, along with perceived message content and personal acceptability ratings, to construct stimuli for an experimental study. There is no confirmatory hypothesis to be tested in this pre-study, but we may conduct a series of exploratory analyses to characterize the collected stimuli and to compare human-generated advice to advice generated by the Large Language Model GPT-4o. Do people underestimate how much they are influenced by AI moral advice?
design_dependent_variables 1) Advice text: For each scenario, participants write a persuasive paragraph arguing that the focal action is either acceptable or not acceptable.
2) Conveyed acceptability: After writing the advice, participants rate how acceptable the action is according to the content of the advice they have just written (0 = not acceptable at all; 100 = fully acceptable).
3) Personal acceptability: Participants also rate how acceptable they personally find the action (0–100 scale with the same anchors). 		WOA (weight of advice).

In the actual advice condition, WOA is computed as: (judgment_revised - judgment_initial) / (advice - judgment_initial). For the main analysis, we will exclude values that are NA (occurs when initial judgment and advice are identical), and values below 0 or above 1 to ensure comparability across conditions.

In the hypothetical advice condition, WOA is assessed by asking: “To what extent could advice from (a Large Language Model (e.g., ChatGPT)/a previous study participant) change your opinion about this situation?”, scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 100 (fully), rescaled to range between 0 and 1 for main analysis.
study_design_overview Each participant is randomly assigned, for each scenario, to one of two instruction conditions:
1) Argue that the action is acceptable
2) Argue that the action is not acceptable
This assignment is done at the trial level, meaning the same participant may write advice in favor of the action for some scenarios and against it for others. The scenario set is randomized across participants from a larger pool. There are no between-subject conditions. 		2 × 2 mixed design: participants are assigned between-subjects to an advice mode (hypothetical vs. actual) and complete six trials where the within-subjects advice source varies (AI vs. human, randomly drawn at the trial level). Scenarios are drawn from a list of 24 cases (treated as random effect in the analysis).

In the “actual advice” condition, each trial presents a scenario and elicits an initial moral judgment about the scenario (how acceptable is the target action, rated on a scale ranging from 0, completely unacceptable at all, to 100, completely acceptable). Then, an advice text plus the advisor’s numerical acceptability score is presented (human or AI). Finally, participants provide a second moral judgment about the scenario. In the hypothetical condition, participants also read the initial scenario and provide an initial moral judgment. Then they rate how much they think that AI moral advice or human moral advice could change their opinion about this scenario.
statistical_tests The primary purpose of this pre-study is to generate a diverse pool of human-written advice texts, accompanied by acceptability ratings. No confirmatory analyses are planned.

We may conduct the following optional exploratory analyses to better understand the structure and content of the collected advice texts (and compare the results to analyses of similar LLM-generated advice texts):

- Text length (e.g., word or character count)
- Sentiment analysis to classify advice as positive, negative, or neutral
- LLM-assisted coding of moral argument components (e.g., harm, fairness, consequences)
- Semantic embedding and clustering 		Factors use treatment coding with levels ordered condition = c(“hypothetical”,“actual”) and source = c(“human”,“ai”), so the baseline is hypothetical_human.

We compute:

m0 <- lmer(WOA ~ condition + source + (1|id) + (1|scenario), data = dat)
m1 <- lmer(WOA ~ condition * source + (1|id) + (1|scenario), data = dat)

anova(m0, m1)

The hypothesis is confirmed if adding the interaction improves model fit as indicated by the likelihood ratio test (alpha <= 0.05) AND if the interaction coefficient is positive (conditionactual:sourceai > 0), indicating that the actual–hypothetical gap is larger for AI moral advice than for human moral advice).

We follow up with simple effects to further characterize the difference between actual and hypothetical weight of advice for both human and ai moral advice:

emm <- emmeans(m1, ~ condition | source)
contrast(emm, method = “revpairwise”, adjust = “none”)
outliers_and_exclusions Individual responses will be excluded if they:
- Contain no substantive advice (e.g., filler, nonsensical, or off-topic text)
- Contain personal identifying information (e.g., names, contact info)
- Contain content that would be inappropriate or potentially harmful to show to other participants (e.g., graphic violence, hate speech, slurs, or threats)

Participants will be fully excluded if they:
- Fail the instruction check, which asks: “Which of the following is TRUE about this study?” with the correct answer being: “You will write both pro and contra moral advice, depending on the assigned instruction.” They are given two attempts to answer correctly.
- Fail either of two verbal attention checks: 1) Implausible statement (e.g., “I have never taken a survey before, including this one”) → Correct response: Disagree or Strongly disagree, 2) Directed-response item instructing participants to select “Disagree” regardless of content → Any other response indicates inattention
- Submit AI-generated or AI-assisted advice texts, as flagged by GPTZero: All advice texts written by a participant will be pasted together and analyzed as a batch. If GPTZero classifies the output as AI-generated or Human–AI co-created, the participant will be excluded.
- Fail a modified Müller-Lyer illusion test in which the two lines are clearly not equally long (the blue line is indeed clearly longer). Participants will be excluded if they give any other answer than “blue” to the question “Which line is longer?”. 		Individual WOA scores from the “actual” condition will be excluded when they are NA (occurs when initial judgment and advice are identical), and if below 0 or above 1, to enable comparability across conditions.

Participants will be excluded if they fail two simple attention checks (screened out live during survey):
1) Which of these is not an animal? Please select “Elephant”. (Response options: Dog, Cat, Elephant, Chair). Correct response: Elephant.
2) Please indicate how much you agree or disagree with the following claim: I can hold my breath underwater for five hours without any equipment. (Response options: Strongly disagree, disagree, agree, strongly agree). Correct responses: Strongly disagree, disagree.

Furthermore, participants will be excluded if they fail a bot check in the form of a fake optical illusion (designed to screen out LLM-generated responses). They will see a modified version of the Müller-Lyer illusion in which the top line with outward-pointing arrows is clearly longer than the bottom line with inward-pointing arrows. They will be asked which line is longer (response options: blue (top line), red (bottom line), they are equally long. The correct response option is “blue (top line)”, those who respond differently will be excluded from analyses.
sample_size 100 We will recruit 400 participants on prolific.com, inclusion criteria: native English speakers, approval rate of previous submissions at least 95%, not having participated in previous studies related to this project, e.g., pilots and the advice elicitation task. Based on a power simulation using pilot data, the minimal effect size of the interaction that we can detect with sufficient power (81.5%) with this sample size is beta = 0.07.
additional_comments Nothing else to pre-register. Human and AI moral advice (elicited in a separate study and consisting of a text paragraph paired with an acceptability score) is filtered in the following way before being included in the design of this current study: If advisors were prompted to write pro advice for that scenario (argue that the action is acceptable), acceptability scores should be at least 50, inclusive (scale: 0, not acceptable at all, to 100, fully acceptable). If prompted to write negative advice, acceptability scores should be below 50.

After completion of the main study, participants fill in the “attitudes towards AI” scale developed by Stein et al., 2024 (Stein, JP., Messingschlager, T., Gnambs, T. et al. Attitudes towards AI: measurement and associations with personality. Sci Rep 14, 2909 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-53335-2).

Exploratory analyses may examine individual differences and content-level predictors of advice uptake. We might test whether participants with more positive attitudes toward AI show less underestimation of its influence, and whether WOA for AI advisors correlates with demographic variables such as age, gender, or education. For human advisors, we may explore whether their advice is more effective when it aligns with their own moral beliefs, or when it aligns with the participant’s initial moral judgment. We might also examine whether AI and human advisors differ in their effectiveness depending on whether the advice supports or challenges the advisee’s initial stance. Additionally, we may compare the content of human and AI moral advice and explore which textual features (e.g., length, tone, or argument type) correlate with WOA.
