Strohminger, N., & Nichols, S. (2014). The essential moral self. Cognition, 131(1), 159-171. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2013.12.005 Feldman, G., & Wong, C. H. (2025). Essential moral self remains unchallenged: Successful replication of Strohminger and Nichols (2014) with extensions comparing morality to ideology and religion. OSF. doi:10.17605/osf.io/g2zv6
How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

Full text

Abstract

People are often skeptical of AI in the moral domain, yet AI-generated ethical advice can influence moral judgments as much as human advice. Unlike most prior work, which attaches human or AI labels to identical advice, we examined how much real advice written by humans and by AI influences moral judgments, and whether people expect less influence from AI than from human advice. First, we developed 24 realistic everyday moral scenarios and collected over 500 persuasive advice texts from both incentivized human writers (N = 92) and GPT-4o. AI-generated advice was longer, more linguistically complex, more semantically uniform, more virtue-oriented, and less extreme than human advice. Next, a new sample of participants (N = 390) either revised initial moral judgments after receiving human or AI advice or indicated how much they expected such advice to influence them. Participants were equally influenced by human and AI moral advice, revising their judgments by a little under a third of the distance to the advice. Participants who only estimated the influence, however, expected less influence from AI than from human advice. These findings suggest that skepticism toward AI in moral contexts may shape people's expectations about AI moral advice, but not how much they are actually influenced by it.

[div-01]

During the preparation of this work the authors used generative AI (Large Language Models like Claude and GPT) to refine the phrasing of pre-drafted text passages and to shorten text passages. LLM assistance was also partially used in coding and in creating supplementary files (e.g., READMEs). The authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.

Introduction

AI systems are increasingly embedded in contexts that involve recommendation, evaluation, and guidance. Both provider reports and emerging academic research indicate that people use Large Language Models (LLMs) not only for information retrieval and task completion, but also for practical advice and interpersonal support, including coaching, counseling, and related personal concerns (Anthropic, 2025; Chatterji et al., 2025; Manoli et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026). Even when users do not explicitly ask for advice about right and wrong, AI systems can still express values (Hadar-Shoval et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). In recommending actions, weighing considerations, or explaining why one option is better than another, they often convey implicit views about what is fair, acceptable, harmful, or worth prioritizing. This means that exposure to morally relevant AI output may arise not only through deliberate advice-seeking, but also through routine use of these systems for more general guidance. Thus, AI systems are increasingly encroaching into a sphere that was for the longest time considered to be uniquely and distinctively human, central for both personal (Strohminger & Nichols, 2014) and collective identity (Ayala, 2010).

The growing presence of AI in morally relevant forms of guidance raises a natural question: how comfortable are people with artificial systems taking on this role? After all, even if the use of AI for ethical guidance is becoming more common, those who actively turn to such systems for moral advice may still constitute only a small subset of the population, and their behavior may diverge from more general public opinion. Psychological research probing stated opinions and attitudes suggests that this could be the case. In a foundational series of (pre-GPT) studies, Bigman and Gray (2018) found that participants were reluctant to let machines make morally consequential decisions in areas such as medicine, law, warfare, and autonomous driving, a pattern they linked in part to the perception that machines lack the kind of "mind" needed for legitimate moral judgment. This pattern is consistent with broader evidence from Dong et al. (2026), who found across 20 countries that fear of AI is systematically higher when people believe the role requires psychological capacities that AI is perceived to lack. Purcell and Bonnefon (2023) offer a related perspective on resistance to AI in the moral domain by showing that people often see their own moral profile as too peculiar to be accurately captured by a machine. In the realm of moral advice, Myers and Everett (2025) found that people expect artificial moral advisors to be more utilitarian than human advisors and report less trust in them, even when the content of their advice is identical (see also Aydin & Malle, 2024; Claessens et al., 2026). Taken together, these findings point to a fairly robust source-based skepticism toward AI as a moral decision-maker, evaluator, or advisor. Moral contexts may be especially vulnerable to such skepticism because they are commonly understood to depend on precisely such kinds of human capacitiesholistic understanding, fairness, sincerity, or empathy (see also Santoro & Monin, 2023). In this sense, these findings echo the intuition captured by Paul Bloom (2023) in The New Yorker: "Human moral judgment is rich and subtle, emerging through the complex interplay of reason and emotion -not the sort of thing that you'd expect a large language model to understand".foot_0

AI Moral Advice Influences Moral Judgment

At the same time, much of the evidence on AI aversion in the moral domain comes from hypothetical judgments, trust ratings, and responses to stylized scenarios. A different picture emerges from research on how closely AI moral judgment aligns with human judgment, and on how people respond to actual AI-generated moral output. LLMs respond to established manipulations from the moral reasoning literature in ways that broadly track human responses (Almeida et al., 2024), capturing some aspects of human moral judgment well (e.g., in the Moral Machine experiment; Awad et al., 2018; Zaim bin Ahmad & Takemoto, 2025) while diverging in others (e.g., an increased omission bias; Cheung et al., 2025; a stronger prioritization of humans over animals, Jotautaitė et al., 2026). People also evaluate actual AI-generated moral reasoning quite positively. In Dillion et al. (2025), GPTgenerated moral justifications were often rated as similarly strong as, or stronger than, those written by a U.S.-representative sample and by The New York Times' Ethicist column. Using the same materials, Meincke et al. (2026) found that a majority of participants preferred a human advisor before seeing any advice, but this preference reversed after exposure to actual advice.

AI moral advice also shapes people's actual judgments. In studies that presented the same AI-generated advice labeled as coming from either a human or an AI, the advice shifted moral judgments regardless of the label. This holds for trolley dilemmas (Krügel et al., 2023b (Krügel et al., , 2026)), everyday moral conflicts (Landes et al., 2026 , using scenarios from Singer et al., 2019), and sacrificial dilemmas across 12 countries (Claessens et al., 2026). Notably, many participants in Krügel et al. (2023b) reported that they would have reached the same judgment without the advice. People followed algorithmic advice even when the advisor was described as untrustworthy (Krügel et al., 2022), and in Landes et al. (2026) only patently absurd justifications reduced reliance on AI advice. Similar patterns appear in the legal domain, where people took advice into account regardless of source despite rating AI advisors as less trustworthy (Aydin & Malle, 2024; see also Böhm et al., 2023), and for dishonest behavior in an economic game (Leib et al., 2024).

Taken together, these findings suggest that, for better or worse, LLMs have reached a level of perceived moral competence that makes their advice consequential: they not only mirror important aspects of human moral judgment, but can also shape human judgments and behavior much like human advice does.

Expectations vs. Actual Influence: Do People Anticipate the Influence of AI Moral Advice?

The contrast between algorithm aversion on the one hand and comparable uptake of human and AI moral advice on the other raises a question that has not been directly addressed: Do people's expectations about the influence of AI moral advice match its actual influence? Research on advice-taking in other domains suggests that expected and actual reliance on advice can diverge, and that some advice effects persist even after controlling for participants' reported or intentional use of the advice (Logg & Schlund, 2024; Schultze et al., 2017). The algorithm aversion literature raises a more specific question: If people are particularly skeptical of AI as a moral source, do they expect less influence from AI moral advice than it actually has, beyond any general underestimation of advice? This question also has practical significance. If people expect AI moral advice to influence them less than it does, they may engage with AI-generated ethical content with less scrutiny than its actual influence would warrant, which has implications for how such systems should be designed and disclosed. If, conversely, expectations match actual influence, people's skepticism toward AI in the moral domain would not come at the cost of misjudging its influence. Krügel et al. (2023b) provide initial evidence that people underestimate the influence of moral advice, whether it is provided by humans or by AI. However, their study relies exclusively on the trolley dilemma and manipulates only participants' beliefs about the source of the advice, rather than presenting actual human-versus AIgenerated moral advice. Holding content constant while varying source labels allows for a controlled test of source beliefs, but real human-and AI-generated content is likely to differ. The persuasive capabilities of LLMs have been demonstrated extensively for political issues (Bai et al., 2025; Hackenburg et al., 2025 Hackenburg et al., , 2026;; Liu et al., 2026), and given the favorable evaluations people give to AI-generated moral content, even relative to texts produced by expert humans (Dillion et al., 2025), this persuasive advantage may well extend to the moral domain. This makes it especially plausible that people underestimate the influence of AI advice more than that of human advice. Testing this possibility requires a study that includes real advice from both sources and compares actual with expected influence. Logg and Schlund (2024) conducted such a comparison in the non-moral domain (see also Logg et al., 2019). Participants either indicated how much they would rely on human versus algorithmic advice in tasks such as predicting future job performance from CVs, or completed Judge-Advisor-System tasks in which they made an initial estimate, received advice from a human or an algorithm, and then revised their judgment. Although participants were often indifferent or somewhat averse to algorithmic advice in hypothetical reports, they relied on it as much as or more than human advice in actual judgment tasks.

In the moral domain, by contrast, research on algorithm aversion often presents people with hypothetical scenarios, without exposing them to actual AI output (Bigman & Gray, 2018; Purcell & Bonnefon, 2023). Studies that do present actual AIgenerated texts typically ask participants to rate their quality, trustworthiness, and similar features, without measuring how much participants incorporate the advice into their own moral judgments (Dillion et al., 2025; Meincke et al., 2026). When advice uptake is studied, advice is typically labeled as either AI-or human-generated when it is in fact all AI-generated (Krügel et al., 2023b (Krügel et al., , 2026;; Landes et al., 2026) or presumably all human-generated (Aydin & Malle, 2024; Krügel et al., 2022). Moreover, all advice-uptake studies except Landes et al. (2026) rely on a fairly restricted set of stimuli (Claessens et al., 2026; Krügel et al., 2023b Krügel et al., , 2026;; Myers & Everett, 2025). To our knowledge, no study has yet compared the uptake of actual, longer-form moral advice generated by humans and by AI across a rich set of relatable ethical scenarios, while also comparing its actual influence with people's expectations about that influence.

Taken together, these gaps point to two open questions: how much real human and AI moral advice influences moral judgments, and whether people's expectations about this influence match its actual extent, particularly for AI, where skepticism toward algorithmic authority is often pronounced. Addressing these questions matters both theoretically and practically. Theoretically, it clarifies whether algorithm aversion in the moral domain reflects actual resistance to AI influence or merely lower expectations of it. Practically, as AI systems are increasingly embedded in contexts involving moral evaluation and decision support, knowing whether people's expectations about AI moral influence are in line with its actual influence is important for assessing autonomy, designing appropriate safeguards, and anticipating the societal impact of AI-generated moral guidance.

The Present Research

We present two studies. First, we developed a set of 24 realistic moral scenarios based on norm conflicts described in prior research on people's everyday moral concerns (Yudkin et al., 2025). Each scenario centers on a conflict between competing considerations, such as self-interest and obligations to family, for example whether one should lend money to one's sister despite expecting that she may not repay it. We then elicited moral advice, either in favor of or against the focal action, from human writers who were incentivized to be persuasive, and asked them to assign a numerical score to their own advice. We generated the same type of advice and corresponding scores using GPT-4o, and compared the resulting human and AI advice texts.

In a second study, a new sample of participants completed a Judge-Advisor System task using a subset of these scenarios. In the actual advice condition, participants first provided an initial moral judgment, then saw real advice written by a human or generated by AI, and finally gave a second judgment. This allowed us to compute Weight of Advice, a standard measure in the advice-taking literature that captures the extent to which people revise their judgments in response to advice (Bailey et al., 2023; Bonaccio & Dalal, 2006; Sniezek & Buckley, 1995). We compare this condition with a hypothetical advice condition, in which a separate group of participants also saw the scenarios and provided judgments, but did not receive any actual advice. Instead, they reported how much they expected their opinion could be changed by advice from either a human or an AI advisor. This design allows us to address three questions: 1) To what extent are moral judgments actually shaped by realistic human and AI advice in relatable moral scenarios?

2) How much influence do people expect moral advice to have on their judgments? 3) Do they specifically underestimate the influence of AI-generated moral advice?

The third question is especially important because it may help explain the apparent gap between people's stated aversion to AI in the moral domain and the more favorable evaluations they often give to concrete AI-generated moral reasoning. These issues have typically been studied separately; our design examines them together.

Open Science and Ethics

The advice elicitation study is preregistered at https://aspredicted.org/8pt3-dmvd.pdf, and the advice-taking task is preregistered at https://aspredicted.org/ie2xu8.pdf. We confirm that we have reported all measures, all conditions and all data exclusions. All data, materials, and analysis scripts, including video demos and technical pilots of the advice-elicitation study (N = 20) as well as the main advice-taking task (N = 20) are publicly available at https://osf.io/jhr98/overview?view_only=0a4299ecf6364e2c8eeaf15b581f9f8f.

This set of two studies received ethical approval from the Institutional Review Board of [blinded for peer review], approval number LIP-2024-08, prior to data collection.

All participants provided informed consent before participation. They were informed about the study's purpose, the expected duration and payment, that their data would be stored and shared anonymously, and that they could withdraw at any time without penalty.

Advice Elicitation

To set the stage for the main advice-taking study, we conducted an advice elicitation study with the goal of collecting high-quality, human-written moral advice on a range of everyday moral scenarios, to be used alongside AI advice in the later advicetaking study.

Design, Materials, and Procedure

The survey was implemented in Qualtrics. Each participant was presented with three scenarios, randomly drawn from a full set of 24 scenarios. These 24 scenarios were generated by the research team for the purpose of the study, taking inspiration from previous research on everyday moral dilemmas (Yudkin et al., 2025). We aimed for scenarios that involved some sort of norm conflict, for instance between obligations to family and self-interest. In addition, they should feel relatable, i.e., it should be easy to imagine that these scenarios could happen to oneself or to someone in one's social circle. Here are three examples: (Lending Money) Maya's sister, Rachel, recently asked her for a loan to help pay off her debts.

Maya is saving up for a down payment on a house, and lending Rachel money would significantly delay her plans-plus, Maya isn't sure if or when Rachel would be able to pay her back. Rachel has always been there for Maya, and Maya feels obligated to help, but she's also concerned about her own financial security. Maya wonders if it's okay to say no to lending Rachel the money. (Splitting the Bill) Whenever Clara goes out to eat with her friends, they usually split the bill evenly. However, Clara tends to order cheaper meals, and sometimes she ends up paying more than what she actually consumed. This has happened multiple times, and she's starting to feel a bit resentful. Clara doesn't want to come across as petty or stingy, but she also feels it's unfair to keep overpaying. She wonders if it's okay to insist on paying only for what she ordered. (Refuse to Help Friend Move) Ben's friend, Tom, has asked him for help with moving house. Ben is completely free on the weekend of the move and would usually not hesitate to say yes. However, he's noticed that Tom has rarely helped him out in similar situations in the past, often providing reasons for being unavailable. Ben isn't sure if Tom's reasons were valid or just excuses, but it's left him feeling resentful and somewhat exploited. Ben wonders if it's okay to make up an excuse and decline helping Tom with the move.

The full list of scenarios is available in the Supplementary Materials. 12 scenarios were generated with the help of generative AI (GPT-4o, accessed via the web chat interface in July 2024), and 12 were exclusively human-written. We did this to prevent potential effects of surface-level text similarity between scenario and advice in the later main study -if, for instance, all scenarios were AI-generated, AI advice could be more convincing just because it is perceived as more similar in style and hence more fitting to the scenario.

For each scenario, participants were randomly assigned to write advice either pro or contra an action that the agent in the scenario was considering ("Write persuasive advice explaining why it is [not] acceptable for Maya to say no to lending Rachel the money"). This task was incentivized: Participants were informed that their writing would be used in a future advice-taking study, and that they could earn a bonus of 3 if one of their pieces of advice would be among the top 10 percent of the most convincing pieces of advice. In addition, they were instructed to keep their advice concise (rule of thumb: not longer than the scenario itself), and not to include any additional commentary, offensive language, or identifying information. The text had to be 150 characters at minimum.

In addition to generating written advice, we asked participants to translate the advice they wrote into a numerical score (to be used for computing the Weight-of-Advice measure in the main task): "The advice paragraph I have just written conveys that refusing to lend the money is…", answered on a sliding scale ranging from 0 ("not acceptable at all") to 100 ("fully acceptable"). Lastly, we asked for participants' personal opinion on each case: "How acceptable do you personally find it to refuse lending one's sister money in this situation?", also answered on a sliding scale ranging from 0 ("not acceptable at all") to 100 ("fully acceptable"). We asked this in order to give people a chance to express their own opinion, and to make the distinction between personal opinion and the assigned direction of argument in the writing task clear. Furthermore, we are using this measure for exploratory analyses (i.e., is advice more convincing when people argue in the direction that they personally favor?).

Besides conflict scenarios like the example above, four of our 24 scenarios were control cases in which we assumed most people to be clearly in favor of an action's moral acceptability (e.g., occasionally buying plastic water bottles instead of always using a reusable bottle), or clearly against (spreading a bad rumour about a colleague at work because of a minor irritation). We selected one such control scenario for each combination of expected judgment (clearly acceptable vs. clearly unacceptable) and scenario origin (human-generated vs. AI-generated). We included these in order to verify whether any effects found in the main task were restricted to morally ambiguous scenarios, or whether they would also extend to clear cases of moral violations or non-violations.

After three scenarios had been completed, the experiment ended with a debriefing and the assessment of demographic variables (age, gender).

Quality Checks

Participants had to correctly answer an instruction check within two attempts before starting the main task ("Which of the following is TRUE about this study?" Response Options: a) You should write moral advice that reflects your personal opinion, b) You will write both pro and contra moral advice, depending on the assigned instruction (correct response), c) You can use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) to assist with writing your advice, d) Your written advice will only be used for internal analysis and will not be shown to other participants), as well as two attention checks, one before and one after the main task (Attention Check 1: "Please indicate your agreement with the following statement: I have never taken a survey before, including this one." Response options: Strongly disagree (correct), disagree (correct), agree, strongly agree. Attention Check 2: "Some people enjoy warm weather, others prefer cooler climates. This sentence doesn't matter. What does matter is that you choose "Disagree" for this question to show you're reading carefully." Response Options:

Strongly disagree, disagree (correct), agree, strongly agree). Participants who failed the instruction check twice were screened out live during the survey, participants who failed either attention check were paid but excluded after data collection.

To guard against LLM-assisted or fully automated completion of the survey, we implemented the following measures: First, we used Qualtrics' inbuilt captcha function at the beginning of the survey. Second, we presented a modified Müller-Lyer illusion at the end of the survey in which the top line with outward-pointing arrows is indeed clearly longer, and asked participants to indicate which line is longer (also providing a free text field for explanation). Participants who indicated that the bottom line is longer or that both lines were equally long were excluded after data collection.

We informed participants before starting the main task that using AI-tools in this task was prohibited, and that suspected AI-assisted responses would be excluded from the competition for the bonus payment of ￡3. We asked them to confirm that they would not use any AI tools for the completion of this task. After completing the survey, we asked again whether they had used any AI tools (and if so, for what), emphasizing that this would not affect the approval of their submission on prolific.com, but merely inform our interpretation of the data.

In the free text fields for advice-writing, we disabled copy-pasting. Furthermore, we used the AI detection tool gptzero.me after data collection to check participants' texts after data collection. Participants for whom any responses were flagged as AIcreated or human-AI-co-created were excluded.

Participants

101 participants completed the survey on prolific.com. Participants had to be native English speakers, have an approval rate of previous studies on the platform of at least 95%, and not have participated in previous studies using the same materials. Participants were paid ￡3 for an estimated 15 minutes of their time (￡12/hour). Seven participants were excluded for failing the first attention check, one for failing the Müller-Lyer bot check, and one because their text was flagged as AI-generated by gptzero.me. Hence, the final sample consisted of 92 participants (mean age = 42.59 years, SD = 13.24 years, 41 female, 49 male, 2 non-binary). The majority identified as White (70), followed by Black (15), Mixed (4), Asian (2), and Other (1). Most participants resided in the United Kingdom (53) or the United States (29), followed by Canada (6) and South Africa (4).

Results

Participants produced 276 advice paragraphs. While inspecting content, we noticed 20 cases in which advice text and score didn't match (e.g., the text argued that the action was acceptable, but the numerical acceptability score was below 50, or vice versa). We attribute these cases to participant error (misclicking or misunderstanding of the scale). While we didn't anticipate this in our preregistration, we still decided to exclude these cases, since they would lead to confusion when presented to participants in the main task. Hence, we ended up with 256 valid advice texts, on average M = 5.33 (SD = 1.83) texts per combination of scenario and advice direction (pro vs. contra action).

GPT

AI-generated moral advice was produced via the OpenAI API on August 4, 2025 using GPT-4o. In a first step, we prompted the model to generate persuasive pro or contra advice for each scenario, using similar instructions as for human participants (see Supplementary Materials for full prompt). We generated seven advice texts for each combination of scenario and advice direction in order to produce some variation. In a second API call, we let the model assign numerical scores to each advice paragraph, rating to what extent the text expressed that the action is morally acceptable (e.g., "Please answer the following question by providing a NUMERICAL SCORE on a scale from 0 (meaning NOT ACCEPTABLE AT ALL) to 100 (meaning FULLY ACCEPTABLE). Don't provide any additional explanation. The text conveys that Maya refusing to lend Rachel the money is…").

We generated 336 advice texts plus scores using GPT. When inspecting scores, we observed that as with humans, texts and scores didn't always align -i.e., GPT sometimes assigned acceptability scores higher than 50 for texts arguing against the acceptability of the action (or vice versa, although roughly 90% of the 69 mismatched cases were advice texts arguing contra the action paired with a high acceptability score). After excluding the mismatched cases, we ended up with 267 valid pieces of AI advice, on average M = 5.93 (SD = 1.72) texts per combination of scenario and advice direction.

Table 1 shows example advice texts from human participants and from GPT for the lending money scenario. All advice texts are available in the OSF repository.

Exploratory Analyses: How does human and AI moral advice differ?

Because our study used real advice from both humans and AI rather than identical content with different source labels, the two sets of advice may differ in ways beyond their source. To characterize these differences, we conducted four sets of analyses. First, we compared the numerical acceptability scores that accompanied the advice texts, to assess whether the two sources differed in how extreme their advice was. Second, we compared stylistic features of the texts themselves such as length, readability, and use of hedging and first-person language. Third, we used text embeddings to compare the semantic content of the texts, i.e., how typical each text was for its scenario and how similar texts from the same source were to each other. Fourth, we used the extended Moral Foundations Dictionary (Hopp et al., 2021) to compare which moral foundations the texts drew on, and whether they emphasized moral virtues or moral violations. In short, AI advice was less extreme, longer, linguistically more complex, semantically more uniform, and more virtue-oriented than human advice. In Study 2, we examine whether these differences are related to how much participants followed the advice. The analyses were not preregistered and should be understood as exploratory.

Advice Extremity: Figure 1 shows the distribution of advice scores per scenario and direction for both human and AI advice. As the plot shows, AI advice scores were less extreme than scores provided by humans. In the contra condition, AI scores (M = 33.92, SD = 10.12) were substantially higher than human scores (M = 9.07, SD = 10.49), whereas in the pro condition both sources produced high scores (AI: M = 85.96, SD = 9.79; human: M = 92.18, SD = 9.79).

To test these differences, we fitted a series of nested linear mixed models predicting advice scores, with random intercepts for scenarios: a null model, a model adding advice direction (pro vs. contra), a model adding advice source (human vs. AI), and a model adding the source × direction interaction. Models were compared with likelihood ratio tests. Adding advice direction improved fit over the null model (χ²df =1 = 1096.09, p < .001), adding advice source improved fit further (χ²df =1 = 53.79, p < .001), and the source × direction interaction improved fit further still (χ²df =1 = 307.61, p < .001). As the means reported above show, the pro-contra gap was smaller for AI than for human advice.

Figure 1. Means, 95% confidence intervals, and raw data points for numerical acceptability scores (0 = "not acceptable at all" to100 = "fully acceptable") corresponding to the moral advice generated by GPT and humans, per scenario and assigned advice direction (pro/contra). Note: Three combinations of scenario and advice (Designer Bag/pro, Awful kids/contra and Worry about Friend/contra) have no AI advice because GPT either did not argue in the assigned direction in these cases, or advice text and score didn't match (see main text for exclusion rationale).

Stylistic Differences:

To characterize stylistic differences between human and AIgenerated advice, we computed ten text-level features for each advice text: word count, sentence count, average sentence length, average word length, proportion of long words (>6 characters), Type-Token Ratio (TTR), Flesch-Kincaid grade level, proportion of hedging words (e.g., might, could, perhaps, possibly), proportion of first-person pronouns, and number of question marks. Each feature was compared between human and AI advisors using a separate linear mixed-effects model per feature, with AI vs. human as the sole fixed effect and random intercepts for scenario and participant; full descriptives and effect sizes for all ten features are reported in Table 2. AI-generated advice was substantially longer than human advice and contained more than twice as many sentences, though individual sentences were slightly shorter on average. AI texts drew on more complex vocabulary, reflected in longer average word length and a higher proportion of long words, and were rated as harder to read on the Flesch-Kincaid index. AI texts also contained more hedging language, whereas human texts used substantially more first-person pronouns and occasionally included rhetorical questions. All differences were statistically significant.

Semantic Differences:

To complement the surface-level linguistic analyses, we examined the semantic content of advice texts using text embeddings. Each advice text was passed to OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large model via the API, which maps text onto a 3,072-dimensional vector space in which semantically similar texts are located close to one another.

To quantify semantic (dis)similarity we used cosine distance, which measures the angle between two vectors and is scale-invariant (ranging from0 = identical meaning to1 = maximally different). We computed two indices. First, for each scenario we calculated a centroid: the average embedding across all advice texts for that scenario, representing the "typical" content. We then measured each individual text's cosine distance from its scenario centroid: a higher value indicates more idiosyncratic or peripheral content. Second, we computed the mean pairwise cosine distance among all advice texts within each scenario × source combination, capturing how much advisors within the same group agreed semantically.

Human and AI advice occupied different regions of semantic space. AI-generated texts were clustered near the scenario centroid (M = 0.079, SD = 0.022), whereas human texts were more dispersed (M = 0.217, SD = 0.082). A mixed-effects model with random intercepts for scenario and participant confirmed this difference was significant (bAI = -0.139, SE = 0.006, 95% CI [-0.149, -0.128], p < .001). The pattern was replicated in the pairwise analysis: within the same scenario, human advisors produced texts that differed considerably from one another (M = 0.389, SD = 0.054), while AI-generated texts were more similar to each other (M = 0.126, SD = 0.029; bAI = -0.263, SE = 0.010, 95% CI [-0.283, -0.242], p < .001). Together, these results indicate that AI advice is semantically uniform and central, consistently covering content close to the scenario average, while human advice is more varied, possibly reflecting individual differences in perspective and reasoning.

Moral Foundations Analysis:

To complement the semantic embedding analysis, we examined the moral content of human and AI advice using the extended Moral Foundations Dictionary (eMFD; Hopp et al., 2021). The eMFD is a crowd-sourced, probability-weighted lexicon that scores texts on five moral foundations derived from Moral Foundations Theory (Graham et al., 2009): Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, and Sanctity. Unlike earlier dictionary approaches that assign words categorically to a single foundation, the eMFD assigns each word a continuous probability score for each foundation, as well as separate virtue and vice components, enabling a more nuanced characterisation of moral language. Within each foundation, the virtue pole captures language that affirms or upholds the moral concern (e.g., compassion, fairness, duty), while the vice pole captures language that violates or threatens it (e.g., cruelty, discrimination, betrayal). We used this tool to assess whether human and AI advisors differed in the moral foundations they drew on, and whether their advice was more virtue-or vice-oriented; source effects and the source × valence interaction for each foundation are reported in Table 3. Figure 2 provides an overview of results.

Across all advice texts, Care (M = 0.121, SD = 0.017) and Fairness (M = 0.121, SD = 0.019) were the most frequently invoked foundations, followed by Loyalty (M = 0.107, SD = 0.014), with Authority (M = 0.098, SD = 0.013) and Sanctity (M = 0.098, SD = 0.015) least prevalent. Pairwise contrasts confirmed that Care and Fairness did not differ from each other (p = .727), nor did Authority and Sanctity (p = .897), but all other foundation pairs differed significantly (all ps < .001, Holm-corrected).

As shown in Table 3, AI advice scored significantly higher than human advice on Care, Fairness, Loyalty, and Authority, with no significant difference for Sanctity. Decomposing scores into virtue and vice components revealed a source × valence interaction for all five foundations: AI advice was more virtue-oriented than human advice, while for vice language AI scored equal to or lower than human advice across foundations (see Figure 2). Means and distributions for virtue and vice scores for each moral foundation in human and AI advice, scored using the extended Moral Foundations Dictionary (eMFD; Hopp et al., 2021). eMFD scores reflect the average probability that the moral words in a text belong to a given foundation pole. Higher scores indicate that more of the detected moral language is associated with that foundation and valence.

Taken together, human and AI advice differed on every dimension we examined. AI advice was less extreme, particularly when arguing against an action. It was also longer and linguistically more complex, contained more hedging and less first-person language, and was more virtue-oriented in its moral language. Human advice, by contrast, was semantically more varied, while AI advice consistently stayed close to the typical content for each scenario. As a result, the comparison between human and AI advice in Study 2 is a comparison between advice as each source naturally produces it, which differs in several respects beyond its source.

Advice-Taking Task

The goal of this task was to measure how much real human and AI moral advice influences moral judgments, and to compare this influence with the influence expected by a separate group of participants. Based on findings from other domains (Logg & Schlund, 2024), we predicted that people would underestimate the influence of AI advice in particular.

Design, Materials, and Procedure

This study was implemented in jsPsych (De Leeuw et al., 2023) and hosted on cognition.run. It had a 2 (advice mode: actual vs. hypothetical, between subjects) x 6 (scenario, within subjects) design. Participants were randomly assigned to either the actual or the hypothetical advice condition. The six scenarios shown to one participant were randomly drawn from the full set of 24 scenarios, without replacement.

In both conditions, participants first saw the text of one scenario (e.g., the lending money scenario introduced earlier), and were asked for an initial moral judgment: "How acceptable is it for Maya to say no to lending Rachel the money?", rated on a numbered sliding scale ranging from 0 ("not acceptable at all") to 100 ("fully acceptable").

In the actual advice condition, the next page would present an advice text from either a previous study participant or from GPT, arguing either in favor of or against the action's moral acceptability. Both advice source and advice direction were randomly drawn on the scenario level.foot_1 Advice source was always disclosed ("Advice from previous participant" vs. "Advice from AI (GPT-4)"), and the numerical acceptability score was presented below the advice, visualized as a selected value on a sliding scale like the one participants had used on the previous page. After reading the advice and continuing to the next page, participants were asked for a second moral judgment of the case ("Please evaluate the scenario once more"). Scenario and advice could be revisited, and participants made a final moral judgment on the same response scale as earlier.

In the hypothetical advice condition, no advice was presented on the second page of each trial. Instead, participants were simply asked: "To what extent could advice from previous study participants [a Large Language Model (e.g., ChatGPT)] change your opinion about this situation?", rated on a numbered sliding scale ranging from 0 ("not at all") to 100 ("fully"). Whether people were asked about the hypothetical influence of other humans or of AI was randomly drawn on the trial level.

After completing all six scenarios, participants completed a 12-item "Attitudes towards AI" survey (Stein et al., 2024) before the experiment ended with a debriefing and the assessment of demographic variables.

Quality Checks

The survey contained two attention checks. The first appeared after the instructions and asked "Which of these is not an animal? Please select 'Elephant'." The response options were Dog, Cat, Chair, and Elephant, and only selecting "Elephant" was coded as correct. The second appeared after the third scenario and asked participants to indicate their agreement with the statement, "I can hold my breath underwater for five hours without any equipment," using four response options: Strongly disagree, Disagree, Agree, and Strongly agree; only Strongly disagree and Disagree were coded as correct. Failing both attention checks resulted in live exclusion from the survey. In addition, we again used the modified Müller-Lyer illusion as a bot check, and excluded all participants who selected anything other than "blue (top line)".

Participants

401 participants completed the survey on prolific.com. Inclusion criteria were being a native English speaker, having an approval rate of at least 95% of previous surveys on the platform, and not having participated in previous studies using similar material. Target sample size (N = 400) was determined by a power simulation based on pilot data (see OSF repository for code). In a linear model predicting weight of advice from advice mode, advice source, and their interaction, this sample size should yield over 80% power to detect a positive interaction coefficient of 𝛽 = 0.07 (as underestimating weight of advice more for AI than for humans would be indicated by a significant interaction effect in this design).
